extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of images depicting complex everyday scenes of common objects in their natural context, with per-instance segmentations for precise object localization. The dataset contains 91 common object categories, 2.5 million labeled instances, and 328,000 images.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin; Michael Maire; Serge Belongie; Lubomir Bourdev; Ross Girshick; James Hays; Pietro Perona; Deva Ramanan; C. Lawrence Zitnick; Piotr Dollar
extraction.citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollar, and C. L. Zitnick, "Microsoft COCO: Common objects in context," in ECCV, 2014.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created through a pipeline that first harvested a large set of non-iconic images containing contextual relationships and non-iconic object views, then labeled each image for object categories using a hierarchical labeling approach, then labeled, verified, and segmented individual object instances. The work used extensive crowd worker involvement via Amazon Mechanical Turk.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Candidate images were collected primarily from Flickr by searching for pairwise combinations of object categories and object-scene category pairs. In rare cases where enough images could not be found, single-category searches were used with explicit filtering to remove iconic images. Flickr photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords were used.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014 and the second half was planned for release in 2015.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors explicitly removed near-duplicate images detected with [43], grouped images by photographer and date taken to minimize near-duplicates across splits, limited downloads to at most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window, and filtered candidate images to remove invalid or iconic images.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Candidate images were filtered to remove invalid or iconic images. For category labeling, categories were grouped into 11 super-categories in a hierarchical interface to reduce annotation time. For dataset splits, near-duplicate images were explicitly removed and images were grouped by photographer and date taken.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation was performed in three primary tasks using Amazon Mechanical Turk: category labeling, instance spotting, and instance segmentation. For category labeling, workers used a hierarchical interface over 11 super-categories and dragged category icons onto one instance of each present category; 8 workers labeled each image and a category was considered present if any worker indicated it. For instance spotting, workers placed a cross on each instance of a specific category, with priming from the previous stage and a magnifying glass for small instances; each image-category pair was labeled by 8 workers. For instance segmentation, a single worker segmented each instance using a modified interface based on OpenSurfaces, with required category-specific training before participation. Segmentations were then verified by multiple workers, and poor-quality segmentations were discarded and returned to the pool. For dense cases with many instances, after 10-15 instances were segmented, remaining instances were marked as crowds using a single segment. The dataset also added five written caption descriptions to each image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes annotation quality for category labeling by comparing AMT workers to expert workers. Ground truth was computed using majority vote of seven expert workers. The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any expert worker. The paper notes that object category presence is often ambiguous and that experts often disagree due to image ambiguity or disagreement about category definitions. It estimates that over 99% of all object categories not later rejected as false positives are detected given 8 annotators. For segmentation verification, each segmentation was initially shown to 3 annotators; if any annotator marked it bad, it was shown to 2 additional workers, and any segmentation not receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes was discarded.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 workers per image for category labeling; 8 workers per image-category for instance spotting; 1 worker per instance for segmentation; 3 to 5 workers per segmentation for verification; 5 captions per image
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk; expert workers were co-authors of the paper. Several children ranging in ages from 4 to 8 were asked to name every object they see in indoor and outdoor environments to help augment candidate categories.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was split into two roughly equal parts for a faster release schedule. The first half was released in 2014 and the second half was planned for release in 2015. The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release was planned to contain 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test. The authors state that MS COCO will evolve and grow over time and that up-to-date information is available online. They also note that some omitted categories may be added in the cumulative 2015 release.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: People are included as an object category in the images.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance object detection and segmentation algorithms by emphasizing non-iconic images of objects in natural environments and varied viewpoints, and by providing rich contextual information with many objects per image.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper discusses dataset bias indirectly by emphasizing collection of non-iconic images and citing that datasets containing more non-iconic images are better at generalizing. It also notes that models trained on one dataset may not generalize well to another and analyzes cross-dataset generalization between MS COCO and PASCAL VOC.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently only labels "things" and not "stuff." The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories, and segmentations were not collected for 11 categories due to too many instances, ambiguity and difficulty of labeling, confusion with other categories, or too few instances. In dense scenes, after 10-15 instances of a category were segmented, remaining instances were marked as crowds rather than individually segmented. The paper also notes that difficult non-iconic images may act as noise during training if models are not rich enough to capture the appearance variability.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training and evaluating object detection and instance segmentation algorithms on objects occurring in their natural context. The paper provides baseline performance analysis for bounding box and segmentation detection. The released splits are train, validation, and test, with annotations released for train and validation but not for test; test is intended for automatic evaluation via an evaluation server.
